claim: Rhythmic actions benefit from synchronization with external events.
source: Rhythmic actions benefit from synchronization with external events.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established understanding in the field.

claim: Auditory-paced finger tapping studies indicate the two cerebral hemispheres preferentially control different rhythms.
source: Auditory-paced finger tapping studies indicate the two cerebral hemispheres preferentially control different rhythms.
evidence: This statement references findings from prior auditory-paced finger tapping studies.

claim: Fast tapping was defined as auditory-motor synchronization at 2.5 Hz.
source: We measured fMRI and MEG during symmetric finger tapping, in which fast tapping was defined as auditory-motor synchronization at 2.5 Hz.
evidence: This is a methodological definition stated in the abstract.

claim: Slow tapping corresponded to tapping to every fourth auditory beat (0.625 Hz).
source: Slow tapping corresponded to tapping to every fourth auditory beat (0.625 Hz).
evidence: This is a methodological definition stated in the abstract.

claim: The left auditory cortex preferentially represents the relative fast rhythm in an amplitude modulation of low beta oscillations.
source: We demonstrate that the left auditory cortex preferentially represents the relative fast rhythm in an amplitude modulation of low beta oscillations while the right auditory cortex additionally represents the internally generated slower rhythm.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by MEG data presented in the results.

claim: The right auditory cortex additionally represents the internally generated slower rhythm.
source: We demonstrate that the left auditory cortex preferentially represents the relative fast rhythm in an amplitude modulation of low beta oscillations while the right auditory cortex additionally represents the internally generated slower rhythm.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by MEG and fMRI data.

claim: Coupling of auditory-motor beta oscillations supports building a metric structure.
source: We show coupling of auditory-motor beta oscillations supports building a metric structure.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the abstract and supported by connectivity analysis in the results.

claim: Sensory cortices make a strong contribution to hemispheric specialization in action control.
source: Our findings reveal a strong contribution of sensory cortices to hemispheric specialization in action control.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Right-handers typically use the right hand for faster, dynamic movements while the left hand is used for slower movements or static control of hand position.
source: In tasks requiring movements of both hands, right-handers typically use the right hand for the faster, dynamic movements while the left hand is used for slower movements, or even static control of hand position (Sainburg, 2002; Swinnen and Wenderoth, 2004; Serrien and Sovijärvi-Spapé, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The right hand taps relative higher tapping frequencies more precisely than the left hand even in bimanual monofrequent finger tapping.
source: Typically, the right hand taps relative higher tapping frequencies more precisely than the left hand even in bimanual monofrequent finger tapping (Repp, 2005; Ivry, 1996; Peters, 1980).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The left hand taps relative lower tapping frequencies more precisely than the right hand.
source: Conversely, the left hand taps relative lower tapping frequencies more precisely than the right hand (Pflug et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The left hemisphere preferentially controls relative higher tapping frequencies and the right hemisphere preferentially controls relative lower tapping frequencies.
source: This suggests the left hemisphere preferentially controls relative higher tapping frequencies and the right hemisphere preferentially controls relative lower tapping frequencies, but the origins of such hemispheric asymmetries are not known.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from behavioral observations cited in the introduction.

claim: The origins of hemispheric asymmetries in tapping frequency control are not known.
source: This suggests the left hemisphere preferentially controls relative higher tapping frequencies and the right hemisphere preferentially controls relative lower tapping frequencies, but the origins of such hemispheric asymmetries are not known.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that motivates the study.

claim: Brain activity is only subtly lateralized during perceptual tasks.
source: This could represent a consequence of the fact that brain activity is only subtly lateralized during perceptual tasks.
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge about brain lateralization.

claim: Functional lateralization is thought to be amplified once a motor output is required.
source: However, functional lateralization is thought to be amplified once a motor output is required (Ivry and Robertson, 1998; Keller and Kell, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Both 2.5 Hz and 0.625 Hz frequencies fall into the natural range of finger movements but represent different ends of the spectrum.
source: Both frequencies fall into the natural range of finger movements but represent different ends of the spectrum (Parncutt and Cohen, 1995; London, 2012; Drake and Palmer, 2000; Repp, 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Movement is known to suppress beta oscillations and to increase activity in the gamma range.
source: Movement is known to suppress beta oscillations and to increase activity in the gamma range (Muthuraman et al., 2012; Tamás et al., 2018; Pfurtscheller et al., 2003; Pfurtscheller and Lopes da Silva, 1999; Engel and Fries, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Neural oscillations in the beta range are implicated in internal timing, especially during rhythm processing.
source: Yet, neural oscillations are, particularly in the beta range, not only reflected current motor state but also implicated in internal timing, especially during rhythm processing, and are amplitude-modulated during rhythm perception and production not only in the motor and supplementary motor cortex, but also in the auditory and auditory association cortex (Arnal and Giraud, 2012; Doelling and Poeppel, 2015; Nobre et al., 2007; Fujioka et al., 2015; Meijer et al., 2016; Morillon et al., 2014; Kilavik et al., 2013; Kulashekhar et al., 2016; Morillon and Baillet, 2017; Iversen et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: There was a significant interaction between condition and hand for timing variability (F(1,41) = 10.23, p=0.003).
source: A two-factor repeated measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) on timing variability across condition (slow and fast bimanual tapping) and hand (left and right) revealed expectedly an interaction between condition and hand (F(1,41) = 10.23, p=0.003).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: Fast tapping was more precise with the right than the left hand.
source: Fast tapping was more precise with the right than the left hand (right hand: mean(M)=13.29 ms, standard deviation (SD) = 2.74 ms; left hand: M = 14.41 ms, SD = 2.78 ms)
evidence: This is a behavioral finding supported by statistical data and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Slow tapping was more precise with the left compared to the right hand.
source: and slow tapping was more precise with the left compared to the right hand (right hand: M = 33.78 ms, SD = 18.42 ms; left hand: M = 31.70 ms, SD = 14.97 ms, see Figure 3).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding supported by statistical data and shown in Figure 3.

claim: There was a main effect of condition with overall higher precision in fast compared to slow tapping (F(1,41) = 108.54, p<0.001).
source: There was a main effect of condition (F(1,41) = 108.54, p<0.001) with an overall higher precision in fast (M = 13.85 ms, SD = 2.80 ms) compared to slow tapping (M = 32.74 ms, SD = 16.90 ms) (Repp, 2005).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: Activity in the auditory association cortex was right lateralized during slow compared to fast tapping (p<0.001, FWE cluster-level corrected, cluster size 395 voxels).
source: Activity in the auditory association cortex was right lateralized during slow compared to fast tapping (p<0.001, FWE cluster-level corrected, cluster size 395 voxels) and this was the only cortical patch that showed lateralized activity (all other p>0.05, FWE cluster-level corrected).
evidence: This is a primary fMRI finding shown in Figure 5 and Table 1.

claim: The auditory association cortex was the only cortical patch that showed lateralized activity.
source: Activity in the auditory association cortex was right lateralized during slow compared to fast tapping (p<0.001, FWE cluster-level corrected, cluster size 395 voxels) and this was the only cortical patch that showed lateralized activity (all other p>0.05, FWE cluster-level corrected).
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI lateralization analysis.

claim: Generation of the slow rhythm activated additionally the bilateral fronto-mesial cortex including the SMA.
source: Generation of the slow rhythm activated additionally the bilateral fronto-mesial cortex including the SMA (see Figure 5 and Table 1).
evidence: This is an fMRI finding shown in Figure 5 and Table 1.

claim: In all three areas (SMA and both auditory association cortices), slow compared with fast tapping increased power in the low [14–20 Hz] and high beta band [21–30 Hz] but not in the delta, theta, alpha, or gamma range.
source: In all three areas (SMA and both auditory association cortices), slow compared with fast tapping increased power in the low [14–20 Hz] and high beta band [21–30 Hz] but not in the delta, theta, alpha, or gamma range (see Table 2).
evidence: This is an MEG finding supported by data in Table 2.

claim: Condition differences were stronger in the low compared to the high beta band in the SMA and in the right A2.
source: Condition differences were stronger in the low compared to the high beta band in the SMA and in the right A2 (SMA: t(16) = 3.033, p=0.002, p=0.818, right A2: t(16) = 1.907, p=0.046), but not in the left A2 (left A2: t(16) = 0.228)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the MEG power spectral density analysis.

claim: The internal generation of the slow rhythm during slow tapping increased low beta power compared to fast tapping in both auditory association cortices.
source: The internal generation of the slow rhythm during slow tapping increased low beta power compared to fast tapping, during which beta power was strongly suppressed, in both auditory association cortices (main effect of condition F(1,16) = 7.267, p=0.011, permutation ANOVA on mean values over the low beta band).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the MEG analysis.

claim: Low beta power condition differences between slow and fast tapping were larger in the right compared to the left auditory cortex.
source: Notably, low beta power condition differences between slow and fast tapping were larger in the right compared to the left auditory cortex (interaction between condition and hemisphere F(1,16) = 3.460, p=0.045) possibly explaining the right-lateralized activation of this cortical region in fMRI.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the MEG analysis that provides an explanation for the fMRI finding.

claim: During slow tapping, low beta power was maximal at beat position one and decreased to maximal beta suppression at the tap on beat position four in both the left and right auditory association cortex.
source: During slow tapping, low beta power was maximal at beat position one and decreased to maximal beta suppression at the tap on beat position four in both the left and right auditory association cortex (red curves in Figure 6).
evidence: This is an MEG finding shown in Figure 6.

claim: The temporal modulation at the fast auditory beat frequency (2.5 Hz) was stronger in the left than in the right auditory association cortex during slow tapping.
source: In the spectral domain, this translated to a stronger temporal modulation at the fast auditory beat rate in the left compared to the right auditory cortex during slow tapping (t(16) = 1.8956, p=0.037).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the MEG spectral analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Low beta power modulation at the slow tapping rate was stronger in the right compared to the left auditory association cortex.
source: In contrast, low beta power modulation at the slow tapping rate was stronger in the right compared to the left auditory association cortex (t(16) = 1.636, p=0.040).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the MEG spectral analysis.

claim: In the fast tapping condition, beta power was maximally suppressed during the entire sequence of four beats.
source: In the fast tapping condition, during which participants actively tapped to every auditory beat, beta power was maximally suppressed during the entire sequence of four beats (blue curves in Figure 6, upper panels).
evidence: This is an MEG finding shown in Figure 6.

claim: Low beta power in the SMA decreased linearly from start of the sequence to the fourth beat position in the slow tapping condition.
source: While auditory-motor synchronization in fast tapping decreased low beta power at every beat position, low beta power in the SMA decreased linearly from start of the sequence to the fourth beat position in the slow tapping condition.
evidence: This is an MEG finding shown in Figure 7.

claim: The SMA spectrum contained a strong peak around 0.625 Hz (amplitude = 0.357 a.u.), but no peak at 2.5 Hz during slow tapping.
source: Consequently, the SMA spectrum contained a strong peak around 0.625 Hz (amplitude = 0.357 a.u.), but no peak at 2.5 Hz during slow tapping.
evidence: This is a result from the spectral analysis of the SMA signal.

claim: During fast tapping there was a strong modulation at 2.5 Hz (amplitude = 0.695 a.u.) and only a very weak modulation around 0.625 Hz (amplitude = 0.058 a.u.) in the SMA.
source: During fast tapping there was a strong modulation at 2.5 Hz (amplitude = 0.695 a.u.) and only a very weak modulation around 0.625 Hz (amplitude = 0.058 a.u.).
evidence: This is a result from the spectral analysis of the SMA signal.

claim: The primary hand motor cortices, cerebellum and the SMA coded solely the motor output in the amplitude modulation of low beta oscillations.
source: Together, in contrast to the auditory association cortices, the primary hand motor cortices, cerebellum and the SMA coded solely the motor output in the amplitude modulation of low beta oscillations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the MEG analysis comparing motor and auditory regions.

claim: In the right auditory association cortex, the amplitude modulation during too long inter-tap-intervals was larger compared to the power modulation during too short inter-tap-intervals.
source: In the right auditory association cortex, the amplitude modulation during too long inter-tap-intervals was larger compared to the power modulation during too short inter-tap-intervals in the sense that low beta power was enhanced at beat position one when participants produced a too long inter-tap-interval (Figure 8, left middle panel, significant cluster at 560–660 ms, p=0.042).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the single-trial analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: Too long inter-tap-intervals during slow tapping were associated with a longer low beta suppression at the end of the sequence coinciding with the delayed tap in the SMA.
source: In the SMA, low beta amplitude at beat position one did not influence performance during slow tapping significantly. Instead, too long inter-tap-intervals during slow tapping were associated with a longer low beta suppression at the end of the sequence coinciding with the delayed tap (Figure 8, right middle panel, significant cluster at 1400–1470 ms, p=0.033; significant cluster at 1560–1800 ms p=0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the single-trial analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: During fast tapping, low beta amplitude coded performance in the SMA.
source: During fast tapping, low beta amplitude coded performance in the SMA. A permutation analysis on fast tapping sequences revealed amplitude coding with enhanced beta power modulations for too long inter-tap-intervals and reduced beta power modulations for too short inter-tap-intervals (Figure 8, rightmost panel, p=0.002).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the single-trial analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: Both slow and fast tapping increased TPDC between the auditory cortices and the SMA in the low beta and mid gamma range with strongest effective connectivity from the left auditory association cortex to the SMA.
source: Both slow and fast tapping increased TPDC between the auditory cortices and the SMA in the low beta and mid gamma range with strongest effective connectivity from the left auditory association cortex to the SMA (see Figure 9).
evidence: This is a finding from the connectivity analysis shown in Figure 9.

claim: There was a main effect of hemisphere (F(1,16) = 7.00, p=0.018) with stronger condition differences between slow and fast tapping in the left (M = 0.007, SD = 0.0048) compared to the right (M = 0.003, SD = 0.0054) hemisphere.
source: A two-factor repeated measures ANOVA on averaged connectivity in the low-beta band across hemisphere (left and right) and direction (auditory to motor and motor to auditory) revealed a main effect of hemisphere (F(1,16) = 7.00, p=0.018) with stronger condition differences between slow and fast tapping in the left (M = 0.007, SD = 0.0048) compared to the right (M = 0.003, SD = 0.0054) hemisphere.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the connectivity analysis.

claim: The connections from left A2 to the SMA, from the right A2 to the SMA, and from the SMA to the left A2 increased low-beta connectivity for slow compared to fast tapping.
source: While the connections from left A2 to the SMA (t(16) = 4.174, p=0.002), from the right A2 to the SMA (t(16) = 2.988, p=0.005), and the one from the SMA to the left A2 (t(16) = 3.385, p=0.001) increased low-beta connectivity for slow compared to fast tapping, the connection from the SMA to the right A2 was not enhanced for slow compared to fast tapping (t(16) = −0.882, p=0.392, see Figure 10, left panel).
evidence: These are statistical results from the connectivity analysis shown in Figure 10.

claim: The connection from the SMA to the right A2 was not enhanced for slow compared to fast tapping.
source: While the connections from left A2 to the SMA (t(16) = 4.174, p=0.002), from the right A2 to the SMA (t(16) = 2.988, p=0.005), and the one from the SMA to the left A2 (t(16) = 3.385, p=0.001) increased low-beta connectivity for slow compared to fast tapping, the connection from the SMA to the right A2 was not enhanced for slow compared to fast tapping (t(16) = −0.882, p=0.392, see Figure 10, left panel).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the connectivity analysis shown in Figure 10.

claim: An increased connection strength in the connection from the SMA to the left A2 during slow compared to fast tapping correlated with reduced timing variability of the right hand when tapping slowly (r = −0.490. p=0.04).
source: An increased connection strength in the connection from the SMA to the left A2 during slow compared to fast tapping correlated twith timing variability in the sense that it reduced timing variability of the right hand when tapping slowly (r = −0.490. p=0.04).
evidence: This is a correlation result from the connectivity-behavior analysis.

claim: The effective connectivity in the low beta range for slow compared to fast tapping was amplitude-modulated by a theta rhythm at 6.5 Hz in all connections except for the connection from the SMA to the right auditory association cortex.
source: The effective connectivity in the low beta range for slow compared to fast tapping was amplitude-modulated by a theta rhythm at 6.5 Hz in all connections except for the connection from the SMA to the right auditory association cortex (for statistics see Table 3), the connection that also did not show significant low beta band condition effects.
evidence: This is a finding from the time-frequency analysis of connectivity with statistics in Table 3.

claim: There was an additional modulation of effective connectivity in the low beta range by an alpha rhythm at 10.5 Hz in all connections except for the connection from the right auditory cortex to the SMA.
source: There was an additional modulation of effective connectivity in the low beta range by an alpha rhythm at 10.5 Hz in all connections except for the connection from the right auditory cortex to the SMA.
evidence: This is a finding from the time-frequency analysis of connectivity.

claim: The auditory association cortex is the part of the brain that represents relative rhythms differently in the two hemispheres.
source: Our experiments identify the auditory association cortex as the part of the brain that represents relative rhythms differently in the two hemispheres.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The left auditory association cortex represents the fast auditory beat rate more strongly than the right auditory association cortex in an amplitude modulation of low beta oscillations during slow tapping.
source: During auditory-paced slow bimanual tapping, when two interrelated rhythms have to be represented by the brain, the left auditory association cortex represents the fast auditory beat rate more strongly than the right auditory association cortex in an amplitude modulation of low beta oscillations, although both auditory cortices receive identical sensory input.
evidence: This is a primary finding discussed in the context of the results.

claim: Both auditory cortices receive identical sensory input during the task.
source: During auditory-paced slow bimanual tapping, when two interrelated rhythms have to be represented by the brain, the left auditory association cortex represents the fast auditory beat rate more strongly than the right auditory association cortex in an amplitude modulation of low beta oscillations, although both auditory cortices receive identical sensory input.
evidence: This is a methodological fact about the experimental design.

claim: The right auditory association cortex increases low beta power more strongly for slow compared to fast tapping than the left auditory association cortex.
source: While both auditory association cortices represent also the internally generated slow tapping rate in an amplitude modulation of low beta power, the right auditory association cortex increases low beta power more strongly for slow compared to fast tapping and activates more strongly in terms of BOLD than the left auditory association cortex.
evidence: This is a finding from both MEG and fMRI analyses.

claim: The brain represents the faster rhythm preferentially in the left and the slower rhythm preferentially in the right hemisphere.
source: This suggests that the brain represents the faster rhythm preferentially in the left and the slower rhythm preferentially in the right hemisphere which ultimately results in different tapping precision of the left and right hand during slow and fast tapping, respectively.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings linking neural and behavioral results.

claim: A functional lateralization in terms of differences in activation of functional homologues was only observed in the auditory and not in the motor association cortices.
source: A functional lateralization in terms of differences in activation of functional homologues was only observed in the auditory and not in the motor association cortices.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the fMRI analysis.

claim: Motor cortices mirrored the actual motor output with a stronger BOLD signal in the bilateral SMA associated with reduced beta suppression during internal timing compared to auditory-motor synchronization.
source: Together with the cerebellum, motor cortices rather mirrored the actual motor output with a stronger BOLD signal in the bilateral SMA associated with reduced beta suppression during internal timing compared to auditory-motor synchronization (Gompf et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from the combined fMRI and MEG analysis with a citation to related work.

claim: The lack of lateralization effects in the motor cortices suggests that the observed functional lateralization on the behavioral level was timing-related and not related to bimanual motor coordination.
source: The lack of lateralization effects in the motor cortices in our study suggests that the observed functional lateralization on the behavioral level was timing-related and not related to bimanual motor coordination (Serrien et al., 2003).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the absence of motor cortex lateralization with a citation to related work.

claim: Right lateralization of auditory association cortex activity was related to improved left hand timing despite a bilateral activation of the SMA in slow tapping.
source: Indeed, right lateralization of auditory association cortex activity was related to improved left hand timing despite a bilateral activation of the SMA in slow tapping.
evidence: This is a conclusion linking the neural findings to behavioral performance.

claim: The nearly absent fast auditory beat rate representation in the right auditory association cortex likely constitutes the consequence of dynamic attention to every fourth auditory stimulus.
source: Because both auditory cortices receive the same auditory input (the fast auditory beat rate) in both slow and fast tapping, the nearly absent fast auditory beat rate representation in the right auditory association cortex likely constitutes the consequence of dynamic attention to every fourth auditory stimulus.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings based on the experimental design.

claim: The right auditory association cortex actively selects the relevant auditory beats for slow rhythm generation.
source: Notably, this filtering is performed in the temporal domain, suggesting that the right auditory association cortex actively selects the relevant auditory beats for slow rhythm generation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Beta power in the right but not in the left auditory association cortex explained timing variability during slow tapping.
source: Beta power in the right but not in the left auditory association cortex explained timing variability during slow tapping.
evidence: This is a finding from the single-trial analysis relating neural activity to behavior.

claim: Time information was coded in the amplitude of beta oscillations in this experiment.
source: In our experiment, time information was coded in the amplitude of beta oscillations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of beta oscillations.

claim: The brain uses the motor system for subsecond timing and non-motor cortices for suprasecond timing.
source: The association between timing variability and amplitude coding in the motor association cortex during fast tapping and the relationship between timing variability and amplitude coding in the right but not left auditory association cortex during slow tapping confirms that the brain uses the motor system for subsecond timing and non-motor cortices for suprasecond timing (Morillon et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings with a citation to related work.

claim: Perceiving syncopated compared to non-syncopated rhythms activates the right more than the left auditory association cortex.
source: Perceiving syncopated compared to non-syncopated rhythms activates the right more than the left auditory association cortex (Herdener et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The involvement of the right auditory cortex is not a direct consequence of the increased complexity of rhythmic grouping during syncopated slow tapping compared to simple auditory-motor synchronization during fast tapping.
source: They rather indicate that the involvement of the right auditory cortex is not a direct consequence of the increased complexity of rhythmic grouping during syncopated slow tapping compared to simple auditory-motor synchronization during fast tapping.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The two rhythms are represented systematically with a stronger representation of the relative fast rhythm in the left and of the relative slow rhythm in the right hemisphere.
source: Instead, the MEG and behavioral results demonstrate that the two rhythms are not represented randomly in the left and right hemispheres, but rather systematically with a stronger representation of the relative fast rhythm in the left and of the relative slow rhythm in the right hemisphere.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined MEG and behavioral findings.

claim: Tapping rhythms were most strongly represented in the low beta band in both motor and auditory cortices.
source: Tapping rhythms were most strongly represented in the low beta band in both motor and auditory cortices.
evidence: This is a finding from the MEG frequency analysis.

claim: Beta oscillations are particularly strong in the motor system including the basal ganglia, which also play an important role in rhythmic motor behavior.
source: Beta oscillations are particularly strong in the motor system including the basal ganglia, which also play an important role in rhythmic motor behavior (Kotz et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The internal representation of the slow tapping rhythm in the right auditory association cortex was not associated with additional top-down signals in the low beta band from the SMA to the right auditory association cortex compared to fast tapping.
source: However, the internal representation of the slow tapping rhythm in the right auditory association cortex was not associated with additional top-down signals in the low beta band from the SMA to the right auditory association cortex compared to fast tapping during which no additional rhythm was represented.
evidence: This is a finding from the connectivity analysis.

claim: Slow tapping increased information flow in the low beta band only from the auditory association cortex to the SMA in the right hemisphere.
source: In the right hemisphere, slow tapping increased information flow in the low beta band only from the auditory association cortex to the SMA, possibly to provide slow rhythm information.
evidence: This is a finding from the connectivity analysis with an interpretation.

claim: The SMA received stronger low beta input from the left auditory association cortex during slow compared to fast tapping which could reflect the effort to integrate the slow with the fast rhythm.
source: The SMA received also stronger low beta input from the left auditory association cortex during slow compared to fast tapping which could reflect the effort to integrate the slow with the fast rhythm that was more strongly represented in the left auditory association cortex.
evidence: This is a finding from the connectivity analysis with a speculative interpretation.

claim: The SMA could be interpreted as the midline structure that integrates rhythm information from both auditory association cortices and times tapping accordingly.
source: The SMA could thus be interpreted as the midline structure that integrates rhythm information from both auditory association cortices and times tapping accordingly.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the SMA's role based on the connectivity findings.

claim: Slow tapping strengthened the top-down connection from the SMA to the left auditory association cortex compared to fast tapping.
source: Yet, in contrast to the right hemisphere, slow tapping also strengthened the top-down connection from the SMA to the left auditory association cortex compared to fast tapping.
evidence: This is a finding from the connectivity analysis.

claim: The left-lateralized top-down connection from the SMA to the left auditory association cortex was the only connectivity that correlated with tapping accuracy.
source: This left-lateralized top-down connection was the only connectivity in our study that correlated with tapping accuracy.
evidence: This is a finding from the connectivity-behavior correlation analysis.

claim: The stronger the connection from the SMA to the left auditory association cortex during slow compared with fast tapping, the more precise participants tapped with their right hand in the slow tapping condition.
source: The stronger the connection was from the SMA to the left auditory association cortex during slow compared with fast tapping, the more precise participants tapped with their right hand in the slow tapping condition.
evidence: This is a finding from the connectivity-behavior correlation analysis.

claim: The right hand may benefit from bidirectional auditory-motor interactions in the left hemisphere when tapping slowly.
source: This suggests that the right hand, that taps fast rhythms more precisely than slow rhythms, may benefit from bidirectional auditory-motor interactions in the left hemisphere when tapping slowly.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the connectivity-behavior correlation findings.

claim: The auditory-motor loop in the left hemisphere may facilitate rhythm integration.
source: Together with the overall stronger directed connectivity between the left auditory association cortex and the SMA, this auditory-motor loop may facilitate rhythm integration in the left hemisphere (Nozaradan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the connectivity findings with a citation to related work.

claim: Beta signals associated with slow compared to fast tapping between the auditory association cortices and the SMA were modulated by a theta rhythm.
source: Beta signals associated with slow compared to fast tapping between the auditory association cortices and the SMA and vice versa were modulated by a theta rhythm.
evidence: This is a finding from the time-frequency analysis of connectivity.

claim: Fronto-temporal theta oscillations have been associated with auditory-motor and multisensory integration.
source: Fronto-temporal theta oscillations have been associated with auditory-motor and multisensory integration (van Atteveldt et al., 2014) and more specifically support auditory working memory (Albouy et al., 2017), speech perception (Assaneo and Poeppel, 2018), and speech production (Behroozmand et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The auditory-motor theta rhythm observed in this finger tapping study was observed at a peak frequency of 6.5 Hz.
source: The auditory-motor theta rhythm observed in this finger tapping study was observed at a peak frequency of 6.5 Hz, which corresponds to the frequency at which also the velocity of slow finger movements is modulated (Gross et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a finding from the time-frequency analysis with a citation to related work.

claim: The observed functional differences between the hemispheres during auditory-paced finger tapping are reminiscent of asymmetries observed during speech processing.
source: The observed functional differences between the hemispheres during auditory-paced finger tapping remind the asymmetries observed during speech processing.
evidence: This is a comparison drawn between the current findings and speech processing literature.

claim: During speech perception, the syllable rate in the theta range serves as a strong acoustic cue that entrains oscillations in the bilateral auditory association cortex and induces auditory-motor interactions in this frequency range.
source: During speech perception, the syllable rate in the theta range serves as a strong acoustic cue that entrains oscillations in the bilateral auditory association cortex and induces auditory-motor interactions in this frequency range (Assaneo and Poeppel, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Auditory-motor interactions are left-lateralized both during speech perception and speech production.
source: Auditory-motor interactions are left-lateralized both during speech perception (Mottonen et al., 2014; Murakami et al., 2015; Hickok, 2015) and speech production (Kell et al., 2011; Keller and Kell, 2016) suggesting left-lateralized auditory-motor loops.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: In both motor and auditory association cortices, binding of speech-relevant rhythms via cross-frequency coupling is left lateralized in fronto-temporal cortices during speech perception.
source: In both motor and auditory association cortices, binding of speech-relevant rhythms via cross-frequency coupling is left lateralized in fronto-temporal cortices during speech perception (Gross et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Left-lateralized auditory-motor loops could improve rhythm integration by cross-frequency coupling both during speech perception and production.
source: These observations suggest left-lateralized auditory-motor loops could improve rhythm integration by cross-frequency coupling both during speech perception and production.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the current findings and speech processing literature.

claim: Reduced auditory-motor coupling in the left hemisphere of people who stutter is associated with overt deficits in controlling speech rhythm.
source: Indeed, reduced auditory-motor coupling in the left hemisphere of people who stutter is associated with overt deficits in controlling speech rhythm (Neef et al., 2015; Chang and Zhu, 2013; Kell et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Representing two rhythms during syncopation lateralizes processing of the relative faster rhythm to the left and the relative slower rhythm to the right hemisphere.
source: We show here that representing two rhythms during syncopation lateralizes processing of the relative faster rhythm to the left and the relative slower rhythm to the right hemisphere.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.

claim: Auditory association cortices filter adaptively the preferred temporal modulation rate and send this time signal to the SMA for motor output coordination.
source: Auditory association cortices filter adaptively the preferred temporal modulation rate and send this time signal to the SMA for motor output coordination.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined findings of the study.

claim: The filter in auditory association cortices is relative rather than absolute, meaning that the hemispheres do not lose the complementary information, but nevertheless represent preferentially different rhythms.
source: The filter is relative rather than absolute, meaning that the hemispheres do not lose the complementary information, but nevertheless represent preferentially different rhythms.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings regarding the nature of hemispheric filtering.

claim: An additional top-down communication from the SMA to the left auditory association cortex may privilege the left hemisphere in integrating multiple rhythms in a multiplexed Gestalt.
source: An additional top-down communication from the SMA to the left auditory association cortex may privilege the left hemisphere in integrating multiple rhythms in a multiplexed Gestalt, which likely represents a prerequisite for more complex cognitive functions like speech processing.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion about the functional significance of the left-lateralized connectivity.

claim: Twenty-five participants (10 males; aged 19–31 years; M = 24 years) were included in the fMRI study.
source: Twenty-five participants (10 males; aged 19–31 years; M = 24 years) were included in the fMRI study
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the study sample.

claim: Seventeen participants (six males, aged 21–38 years; M = 26 years) were included in the MEG study.
source: seventeen participants (six males, aged 21–38 years; M = 26 years) in the MEG study.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the study sample.

claim: All participants were right-handed according to self-reports and their laterality index based on the Edinburg inventory of manual preference (fMRI: M = 86; MEG: M = 89).
source: Participants had normal or corrected-to-normal visual acuity, normal hearing, no neurological deficits and were right-handed according to self-reports and their laterality index based on the Edinburg inventory of manual preference (fMRI: M = 86; MEG: M = 89; Oldfield, 1971).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about participant characteristics with a citation to the handedness inventory.

claim: In every trial, 36 auditory beats (1600 Hz, 2 ms) were presented with a constant inter-beat-interval of 400 ms (2.5 Hz, 210 bpm).
source: In every trial of this auditory paced finger tapping paradigm, 36 auditory beats (1600 Hz, 2 ms) were presented with a constant inter-beat-interval of 400 ms (2.5 Hz, 210 bpm).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the experimental paradigm.

claim: Auditory input did not differ between conditions.
source: No auditory feedback was provided. Thus, auditory input did not differ between conditions.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the experimental design.

claim: Tapping to the 36 auditory beats resulted in 36 taps when tapping the fast rate and nine taps when tapping the slow rate during each 15 second-long trial.
source: Therefore, tapping to the 36 auditory beats resulted in 36 taps when tapping the fast rate and nine taps when tapping the slow rate during each 15 second-long trial.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the experimental paradigm.
